content_metadata.description: An instructional video demonstrating the method of backward chaining for teaching skills using the example of handwashing. It focuses on reinforcing independent behavior starting from the last step and progressing backward to earlier steps.

qAndA.question: What type of reinforcement is used in the video?

qAndA.answer: Two steps - turning off water, and drying hands.
qAndA.question: How many steps in the handwashing chain does the student complete independently in the first demonstration?

qAndA.answer: The instructor provides less prompting in the second scene, allowing the student to perform more steps independently.
qAndA.question: How does the instructor's level of prompting change from the first scene to the second scene?

qAndA.answer: The reinforcement always falls at the end of the chain, allowing for flexibility with reinforcers.
qAndA.question: What is an advantage of using backward chaining mentioned in the video?

qAndA.answer: The student shows a clear expression of pleasure and satisfaction when receiving the fruit treat.

activities.description: Instructor prompts student to wash hands; student washes hands with instructor's physical guidance.
Student turns off the water independently.
Student takes a paper towel independently.
Student dries hands independently; Instructor praises the student.
Instructor gives the student a fruit treat as reinforcement.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Now let's look at how to perform backward chaining.
The definition of backward chaining is
linking together behaviors beginning with the last behavior in the chain.
Let's go through the procedure with the same example of washing hands
in order to see how this type of chaining differs from forward chaining.
First, prompt your student to perform all the behaviors in the chain in order
except for the last behavior and then reinforce your student's
independent performance of the last behavior. Wash hands!
Okay, we're going to turn water on. Get soap! Rub hands!
Cut, cut, cut, scrub! Rub, rub! Excellent! Water off!
Great job! Your hands are all clean out!
Here is your fruit treat.
In this example, we see the instructor prompting the student to turn on water,
get soap, rub hands, rinse hands, and turn off water.
The instructor stops before the last behavior and the student must complete the
last behavior of drawing hands independently in order to receive reinforcement.
Then, reinforce your student's independent performance of the next to last and last
behaviors in order. Wash hands!
You're going to turn water on. Get soap! Rub your hands!
Rub, rub, rub, rub, rub, scrub, scrub! Great job!
You remember it all by yourself! That's excellent!
Here's your fruit treat!
Now you see the instructor prompts the student to turn on water, get soap,
rub hands, and rinse hands. But then stops so that the student must complete the last two
behaviors of turning off water and drawing hands in order to get the reinforcer.
Then, reinforce your student's independent performance of the last three steps in order
and continue in this manner until your student can complete the entire chain independently
following the SD.
An advantage of using backward chaining is that the reinforcement always falls at the end
of the chain, allowing you to use a variety of reinforcers.
